claims.text: Differences in constituent diffusion kinetics and mixing enthalpies drive Mg segregation during post-processing.
Mg segregates preferentially to grain boundaries and interfaces during mild annealing.
Mg segregation leads to the nucleation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The resulting microstructural changes alter the chemistry and morphology of oxide scales formed during high-temperature exposure and corrosion.
Changes in oxide-scale chemistry and morphology modify corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The initial rapidly solidified alloy is a non-equilibrium, predominantly single-phase solid solution.
Mg and the other alloying elements are initially distributed uniformly.
The initial alloy contains only minor or no intermetallic precipitates.
Thermal exposure at approximately 500–700°C activates diffusion sufficiently to permit the proposed evolution.
Discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates or Mg-segregated interfacial layers act as heterogeneous oxide-nucleation sites.
Atomic-size and mixing-enthalpy disparities between Mg and heavier alloying elements promote local segregation during thermal treatment.
Mg-rich intermetallics preferentially form Mg-based oxides or mixed oxides during subsequent oxidation.
The altered oxide film changes oxygen transport or scale adhesion.
Mild thermal exposure increases the volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallics relative to the initial homogeneous state.
Annealing changes oxide-scale composition, thickness, and adherence relative to the initial state.
The microstructural and oxide-scale changes produce measurable shifts in corrosion rates, oxidation kinetics, and electrochemical responses.
The proposed kinetic phase separation requires sufficiently large constituent-property disparities, particularly those involving Mg.
